title: History as a Discipline: Sources & Skills
description: What history is and why we study it — chronology and key terms, primary and secondary sources, evaluating evidence, and the concepts historians use to explain the past.

notes.heading: What Is History and Why Study It?
notes.body: **History** is the study and interpretation of the human past, built from the evidence that has survived. It is not simply a list of dates and events — it is an ongoing conversation between the present and the past, in which historians ask questions, weigh evidence, and construct explanations. Why study it? First, history explains how the world we live in came to be: our laws, borders, languages, and institutions all have origins in past events. Second, it develops transferable skills — analysing evidence, spotting bias, building arguments, and judging reliability — that are useful in law, journalism, and everyday life. Third, history helps us understand other people and cultures, past and present, and warns us by showing the consequences of past choices, from wars to revolutions. A famous warning attributed to the philosopher George Santayana says that those who cannot remember the past are condemned to repeat it. Whether or not history literally repeats itself, knowing it gives us perspective on our own time.

notes.heading: Chronology and Measuring Time
notes.body: **Chronology** means the order of events in time, and historians need shared systems for measuring it. Dates are labelled **BC** (Before Christ) or **AD** (Anno Domini, "in the year of the Lord") in the older system, and **BCE** (Before Common Era) and **CE** (Common Era) in the modern, religion-neutral system — the numbering is identical. Note that BC/BCE dates count backwards: 500 BCE is earlier than 100 BCE, and there is no year zero, so 1 BCE is followed directly by 1 CE. A **decade** is 10 years, a **century** is 100 years, and a **millennium** is 1,000 years. Centuries are numbered by counting up from year 1, so the nineteenth century ran from 1801 to 1900 — the 1800s. A **timeline** displays events in chronological order and helps you see duration, gaps, and simultaneity (things happening at the same time in different places). Historians also divide the past into **periods** — such as the medieval period (roughly 500–1500 CE in Europe) — and an **anachronism** is something placed in the wrong time, like a wristwatch in a film about Roman gladiators.

notes.heading: Primary and Secondary Sources
notes.body: Everything historians know comes from **sources** — surviving pieces of evidence. A **primary source** was created during the period being studied, by someone who was there: letters, diaries, official documents, coins, photographs, buildings, tools, and oral accounts. A **secondary source** was created afterwards by someone who was not present, using primary sources and other evidence: textbooks, documentaries, museum displays, and historians' books. The distinction matters because primary sources take us closest to the past, while secondary sources already contain someone else's interpretation. However, neither is automatically "better": a primary source may be biased, mistaken, or incomplete, while a good secondary source can draw on far more evidence than any eyewitness had. Some sources sit awkwardly between the two — a memoir written fifty years after the event is primary evidence for the writer's memory but was shaped by everything that happened in between. Skilled historians use both kinds, cross-checking them against each other to build the fullest possible picture.

notes.heading: Evaluating Sources: Origin, Purpose, Bias and Reliability
notes.body: Because sources are created by people with their own viewpoints, historians **evaluate** every source before trusting it. Start with **origin**: who created it, when, and where? Then ask about **purpose**: why was it made, and for which audience — to inform, to persuade, to boast, or to justify? These questions reveal **bias**: a one-sided view that emphasises some facts and ignores or twists others. A victorious king's account of a battle, for example, will probably exaggerate his enemy's losses. **Reliability** — how far a source can be trusted as accurate — is tested by **cross-referencing**: comparing it with other independent sources to see whether they agree. Crucially, a biased source is not a useless source. A wartime propaganda poster is unreliable as a picture of real events, but it is excellent evidence of what a government wanted its people to think and feel. Historians therefore ask not just "is this true?" but "what is this evidence *of*?" — a source can be reliable for one question and worthless for another.

notes.heading: Change and Continuity
notes.body: Two of the historian's most important questions are: what **changed**, and what **stayed the same** (continuity)? Between 1066 and 1500 in England, for example, castles changed from timber motte-and-bailey designs to stone concentric fortresses, yet the underlying structure of society — a king ruling with the support of lords over peasant farmers — showed remarkable continuity. Change can be fast (a revolution, an invasion) or slow (the gradual decline of the Roman Empire over more than a century), and it can affect some groups more than others: the Black Death transformed life for surviving peasants, whose labour became more valuable, while kings and lords remained kings and lords. Historians also look for **turning points** — moments after which things were clearly different, such as the Norman Conquest of 1066 for England. Judging change and continuity fairly means examining several aspects of life (politics, religion, technology, ordinary people's experiences) rather than assuming that one big event changed everything at once.

notes.heading: Cause, Consequence and Significance
notes.body: Historians explain events by tracing their **causes** and **consequences**. A cause is anything that helps bring an event about; a consequence is anything that results from it. Causes are usually layered: **long-term** causes build up over years (such as poverty and hunger before a revolution), while **short-term triggers** spark the event itself (a sudden price rise, a single arrest). Similarly, consequences can be intended or unintended, immediate or delayed for decades. Rarely does one cause explain everything, so historians rank causes and argue about which mattered most. **Significance** is a related judgement: how important was this person or event? An event is usually judged significant if it affected many people, changed lives deeply, lasted a long time, or still shapes the world today. Significance is not fixed — people can be celebrated in one generation and reassessed in the next as values change. Being able to argue "this mattered because…" with evidence is one of the core skills of writing good history.

notes.heading: How Historians Construct Narratives
notes.body: History does not write itself. The past is everything that ever happened; **history** is the selection historians make from it. To produce a coherent account, a historian must choose a question, gather sources, decide which evidence to include and which to leave out, arrange events into a narrative with a beginning, middle and end, and offer an interpretation of what it all meant. Because these choices involve judgement, two honest historians using the same evidence can still reach different **interpretations** — for example, disagreeing over whether a ruler was a strong leader or a cruel tyrant. Interpretations also change over time as new evidence is discovered (archaeology constantly revises what we know) and as each generation asks new questions of the past — modern historians pay far more attention to women, ordinary workers, and colonised peoples than historians did a century ago. This does not mean all opinions are equally valid: an interpretation must be supported by evidence and must deal honestly with evidence that contradicts it. When you read history, always ask who wrote it, when, and why.

flashcards.definition: The study and interpretation of the human past, constructed from surviving evidence rather than being a simple list of everything that happened.
flashcards.example: A historian studying letters and tax records to explain why a medieval town grew wealthy.

flashcards.definition: The arrangement of events in the order in which they happened in time.
flashcards.example: Placing 1066 (Norman Conquest) before 1348 (Black Death reaches England) on a timeline.

flashcards.definition: Before Common Era / Common Era — the religion-neutral way of labelling years, with identical numbering to BC and AD.
flashcards.example: The Roman invasion of Britain in 43 CE (or AD 43).

flashcards.definition: A period of 100 years, numbered from year 1, so the 19th century means 1801–1900.
flashcards.example: The Battle of Waterloo (1815) took place in the nineteenth century.

flashcards.definition: Evidence created during the period being studied, by people who were there — documents, objects, images or oral accounts.
flashcards.example: A soldier's letter home written from the trenches in 1916.

flashcards.definition: An account created after the period being studied, by someone who was not present, using primary sources and earlier work.
flashcards.example: A modern textbook explaining the causes of the First World War.

flashcards.definition: A one-sided view in a source that emphasises some facts while ignoring or distorting others, often because of the creator's purpose.
flashcards.example: A king's chronicle claiming his army was outnumbered ten to one but won through bravery.

flashcards.definition: How far a source can be trusted to be accurate for a particular question, tested by cross-referencing it against other independent evidence.
flashcards.example: Checking a diary's account of a fire against newspaper reports and official records.

flashcards.definition: The twin historical questions of what altered over a period and what stayed the same, and for whom.
flashcards.example: After 1381, peasants won higher wages (change) but the king still ruled England (continuity).

flashcards.definition: A cause helps bring an event about (long-term causes plus short-term triggers); a consequence is what results from it, intended or not.
flashcards.example: The Black Death (cause) led to labour shortages and higher wages for surviving peasants (consequence).

flashcards.definition: A judgement about how important a person or event was — based on how many people were affected, how deeply, how long the effects lasted, and whether they still matter today.
flashcards.example: The invention of printing is significant because it changed how knowledge spread across the whole world.

flashcards.definition: A historian's evidence-based explanation of the past; different historians can reach different interpretations from the same evidence.
flashcards.example: One historian calls a ruler a reformer while another, using the same records, calls him a tyrant.

questions.stem: Which of these best describes what history is?
choices: A complete list of everything that has ever happened
The study and interpretation of the past, constructed from surviving evidence
Memorising dates, kings and queens
Stories about the past that cannot be checked
questions.explanation: History is an interpretation built from evidence. The past is everything that happened; history is what historians select, question and explain using sources, so it can always be checked and argued over.

questions.stem: What does BCE stand for in modern dating?
choices: Before Christian Era
British Common Era
Before Common Era
Before Current Events
questions.explanation: BCE means Before Common Era. It pairs with CE (Common Era) and uses exactly the same numbering as BC and AD — it is simply a religion-neutral label.

questions.stem: An archaeologist uncovers a coin minted during the reign of a Roman emperor. What kind of source is the coin for studying Roman Britain?
choices: A primary source, because it was created during the Roman period itself
A secondary source, because coins are made of metal
A biased source, so it should be ignored
A secondary source, because the archaeologist found it recently
questions.explanation: The coin was made during the period being studied, which makes it a primary source. The date of its discovery is irrelevant — what matters is when and why it was created.

questions.stem: A history book published in 2020 that explains the Roman Empire using archaeological evidence is an example of:
choices: A primary source, because it contains facts
A secondary source, because it was written afterwards by someone interpreting earlier evidence
A primary source, because the author is an expert
Neither a primary nor a secondary source
questions.explanation: The book was created long after the Roman period by an author who was not there and who worked from primary sources — the definition of a secondary source.

questions.stem: How many years are there in a century?
questions.explanation: A century is 100 years. A decade is 10 years and a millennium is 1,000 years — the three standard blocks historians use to measure long periods.

questions.stem: A historian asks: "Who wrote this document, when, and why?" Which part of source evaluation is she carrying out?
choices: Checking the source's origin and purpose
Measuring the source's significance
Establishing chronology
Cross-referencing the source
questions.explanation: Asking who created a source and when establishes its origin; asking why it was made establishes its purpose. These are the first two steps in judging how far to trust it.

questions.stem: A wartime propaganda poster shows the country's soldiers as unbeatable heroes. A historian wants to know what conditions in the army were really like. How useful is the poster?
choices: Very useful — posters always tell the truth about the army
Completely useless — biased sources have no value at all
Useful — it gives an accurate picture of soldiers' daily lives
Not reliable for that question, but valuable as evidence of how the government wanted people to think about the war
questions.explanation: The poster is biased persuasion, so it is unreliable as evidence of real conditions. But bias does not make a source useless — it is excellent evidence of official aims and attitudes, which is a different question.

questions.stem: After the Black Death, surviving peasants could demand higher wages, but England was still ruled by a king and nobles. This is an example of:
choices: Change without any continuity
Continuity without any change
Both change (peasants' bargaining power) and continuity (the structure of government)
A cause and its trigger
questions.explanation: The event changed some aspects of life — labour became more valuable — while the political order stayed the same. Good history examines change and continuity together rather than assuming one event changed everything.

questions.stem: Which of these is a consequence of an event, rather than a cause?
choices: Something that helps bring the event about
A long-term condition that builds up before the event
The trigger that sparks the event
Something that results from the event happening
questions.explanation: A consequence is an outcome — something that happens because the event occurred. Causes (long-term conditions and short-term triggers) all come before the event; consequences come after.

questions.stem: Which of these would be the strongest argument that an event was historically significant?
choices: It is mentioned in a lot of textbooks
It happened a very long time ago
It affected large numbers of people deeply, and its effects lasted and still shape the world today
It involved a famous king or queen
questions.explanation: Significance is judged by the depth, scale and durability of an event's effects, not by fame or age. An obscure event that transformed millions of lives is more significant than a famous one that changed little.

questions.stem: Two professional historians read exactly the same sources about a medieval king, but one calls him a strong reformer and the other calls him a brutal tyrant. What is the best explanation for this disagreement?
choices: One of them must be lying about the evidence
History is only opinion, so both are wrong
Interpretation involves selection and judgement, so honest historians can weigh the same evidence differently
One of them must have secretly used extra sources
questions.explanation: Constructing a narrative requires selecting and weighing evidence, which involves judgement. Reasonable historians can disagree while both staying faithful to the sources — that is why history is an argument, not a fixed list of facts.

questions.stem: How many years separate 400 BCE from 100 CE?
choices: 300 years
400 years
500 years
600 years
questions.explanation: From 400 BCE to 1 BCE is 399 years, then 100 years to reach 100 CE — 499 years in total, usually rounded to 500. The common mistake is simply adding 400 + 100 without remembering there is no year zero; the key insight is that BCE counts down to 1 and CE counts up from 1.

questions.stem: A film about ancient Egypt shows a builder wearing a wristwatch. What is the watch an example of?
choices: A primary source
An anachronism — something placed in the wrong time period
A secondary source
A turning point
questions.explanation: An anachronism is something shown or described in a period before or after it actually existed. Wristwatches were invented thousands of years after the pyramids were built.

questions.stem: A diary claims that "everyone in the city celebrated the new king's coronation." What should a historian do before accepting this claim as accurate?
choices: Accept it, because diaries are primary sources and primary sources are always reliable
Reject it completely, because diaries are always biased
Cross-reference it with other independent sources, since one person's claim about 'everyone' cannot be checked from the diary alone
Assume it is true because it is very old
questions.explanation: A single source, however valuable, records one viewpoint. Cross-referencing against other independent evidence — official records, other accounts, material evidence — is how historians test whether a sweeping claim holds up.

questions.stem: Which of these steps is part of how historians construct a historical narrative?
choices: Including every single fact that is known about the past
Selecting and arranging evidence to answer a chosen question, and offering an interpretation
Copying out primary sources without comment
Inventing details to make the story more exciting
questions.explanation: Historians cannot include everything, so they select evidence relevant to their question, arrange it into an account, and interpret its meaning. Invented details would make the work fiction, not history.
